newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Sanyo enters alternative fuel vehicle race.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Sanyo enters alternative fuel vehicle race.

text.p: Sanyo Electric Co Ltd, which already invests some eight percent of its revenue on environment-minded technology, said on Thursday it has launched a new business aimed at fuelling the world's nascent natural gas vehicle (NGV) industry.

Wagering that the number of NGVs on the road in Japan will rise from current levels of roughly 1,300 to some 200,000 by the year 2000, Sanyo plans to mass-produce NGV refuelling units for home use and use alongside conventional gasoline pumping facilities across the country.
The venture marks the latest drive by a major manufacturer to cash in on the global race for an alternative to conventionally fuelled vehicles.

In late June, Toyota Motor Corp said it planned to begin mass-production of "hybrid vehicles" -- which have a gasoline engine, an electric generator and an electric motor under the same hood -- by the end of the year.
Sanyo said Toyota, along with other carmaking giants Ford Motor Co, General Motors Corp and Honda Motor Co Ltd, is also developing NGVs.

NGVs run strictly on a compressed form of natural gas and are said to emit just four percent of the nitrogen oxide levels and 0.01 percent of the carbon monoxide levels produced by gasoline-powered vehicles.
The clean-burning system is likely to gain increasing popularity as governments continue in their current push for improved air quality, Sanyo said.

The company plans to market small-scale home-use systems capable of refuelling a four-door sedan NGV in about 2.4 hours, as well as larger units that can refuel the same-sized vehicle in just 3.7 minutes.
Already the company has 70 of the smaller pumps in place across Japan.

Sanyo said there are currently about one million NGVs in operation around the world, with some 300,000 vehicles running in Russia, 300,000 in Italy, 50,000 in the United States and another 350,000 in various other countries.
The company said its previous experience with refrigeration compressors and gas appliances made for a smooth transition into the field of natural gas compression pumps.
"This is a natural area of growth for us," said Sanyo director Fusao Terada.
"Natural gas vehicles will likely be best suited to the replacement of larger, diesel-driven vehicles, which need more power than electric power motors can provide," he added.

Asked whether the venture represents a belief by Sanyo that NGVs will be the most successful alternative in the future to conventional vehicles, Terada said Sanyo is also the largest combined producer of nickel-cadmium batteries and nickel-metal hydride batteries, which represent the front-running technology utilised in electric vehicles.
"We hope to be of assistance to many of these technologies," Terada said.
Regarding the safety of NGVs, a Sanyo spokesman said that of 158 NGV accidents reported in a one-year period in the United States, none resulted in fires or explosions.
